"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEl \u003cb\u003epunto:
"

The melting point is the temperature at which solid and liquid coexist. A pure compound melts over a narrow range (0.5–1 °C). It is measured in a capillary tube with a few millimeters of sample, inside a heating block with a thermometer. Two values are recorded: onset (first drop) and end (all liquid).

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEl diagrama T–x muest:
"

The T–x diagram shows the liquidus curve (above it everything is liquid) and the solidus or eutectic line (below it everything is solid). Between them solid and liquid coexist. The observed range corresponds to the vertical distance between both curves at the sample composition.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eLa muestra y el termó:
"

The sample and the thermometer are not in equilibrium if heated fast: the observed value is above the true one and the range appears wider. The recommended approach is to get quickly to ~15 °C below the expected value and then heat at 1–2 °C/min. Use the rate control and compare.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003ePara identificar un d:
"

To identify an unknown, it is mixed with a standard and the mixed melting point is measured. If they are the same compound, the melting point does not change; if they are different, the mixture melts lower and over a wide range. Turn on “Mix with another compound” to simulate it.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eUna impureza soluble:
"

An impurity soluble in the liquid lowers the melting point (freezing-point depression): ΔT ≈ R·Tm²·ximp/ΔHfus. The solid begins to melt at a temperature close to the eutectic and finishes lower than the pure compound: the range broadens. That is why a wide range indicates an impure sample.

"
